```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
library(DALEXtra)
source(here::here("R/theme.R"))
source(here::here("R/data.R"))
```

## Why this matters

You have fitted a random forest that predicts abundance reasonably well, and the next
question — from a supervisor, a reviewer, or yourself — is "so what drives it?". The
conventional answer is a variable-importance plot, and it takes one line of code.

That plot is the most over-interpreted object in applied machine learning. It is routinely
read as a ranking of ecological drivers when it is nothing of the kind: it is a description
of one fitted model's internal arithmetic, it depends on which measure you asked for, and it
has no zero. This page puts two standard measures on the same model and shows them
disagreeing, then fixes the missing zero.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

## What is actually in the data

Because the survey is simulated, we know the answer before we start. From
`R/make-example-data.R`:

| Predictor | True role |
| --- | --- |
| `depth_m` | real, humped, peak at 80 m |
| `temperature_c` | real, humped, peak at 9 °C |
| `chlorophyll_mg_m3` | real, positive, saturating |
| `substrate` | real: mud > gravel > sand > rock |
| `longitude`, `latitude` | proxies for a smooth spatial field no covariate explains |
| `salinity_psu` | **no effect** |
| `survey_year` | **no effect** |
| `season` | no direct effect; drives temperature and chlorophyll |

And we add three columns of our own, drawn from `rnorm()`, which have no effect by
construction and no relationship to anything.

```{r}
#| label: data
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

modelling <- survey |>
  select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu,
         substrate, season, survey_year, longitude, latitude) |>
  drop_na()

set.seed(20)
modelling <- modelling |>
  mutate(noise_1 = rnorm(n()), noise_2 = rnorm(n()), noise_3 = rnorm(n()))

set.seed(4)
split <- initial_split(modelling, prop = 0.5)
train_set <- training(split)
test_set  <- testing(split)

forest_recipe <- recipe(abundance ~ ., data = train_set) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

set.seed(2)
forest <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(forest_recipe) |>
  add_model(rand_forest(trees = 800) |>
              set_engine("ranger", seed = 1, importance = "impurity") |>
              set_mode("regression")) |>
  fit(train_set)

c(train = nrow(train_set), test = nrow(test_set))
```

The three noise columns are the point of the page. They are the **null reference**: whatever
number an importance measure assigns to a column that cannot possibly matter is the number
that measure gives to nothing at all. It is the same habit
[§8 used for clustering](../08-unsupervised-learning/choosing-the-number-of-clusters.qmd)
and [§7 used for model scores](../07-validation/regression-metrics.qmd) — find out what
no-skill looks like before reading the result.

## Measure one: impurity importance

This is the default for trees and forests and the one you get if you ask for importance
without specifying. Every time a tree splits on a variable it reduces the impurity —
for regression, the within-node variance — of the node it split. Impurity importance adds
those reductions up across the whole forest.

```{r}
#| label: impurity
impurity <- extract_fit_engine(forest)$variable.importance

tibble(term = names(impurity), importance = impurity / max(impurity)) |>
  arrange(desc(importance)) |>
  mutate(importance = round(importance, 3))
```

Read down to rank six. `noise_3`, `noise_1` and `noise_2` sit in positions **six, seven and
eight of sixteen** — above salinity, above `survey_year`, and above *every* substrate and
season term. Substrate, which has a genuine effect in the generator, appears at ranks 12, 13
and 16, below all three columns of random numbers. Repeat this on eight different splits of
the data and the picture does not change: the noise columns land between ranks three and
nine every time, and every substrate dummy is below all three of them every time.

This is not a fluke; it is what the measure does. A continuous variable offers hundreds of
distinct split points, so a tree searching for the best split will, by chance alone, find one
that reduces impurity a little. A two-level dummy offers exactly one. Impurity importance
therefore rewards **variables with many possible split points**, regardless of whether they
carry information.

::: {.callout-warning}
Impurity importance (Gini importance, `importance = "impurity"`, the `randomForest` default)
is biased towards continuous and high-cardinality predictors. On this data it ranked pure
`rnorm()` noise above a real categorical effect. Do not use it to rank predictors of
different types against each other.
:::

## Measure two: permutation importance

The permutation measure asks a question with an operational meaning: **how much worse does
this model predict if I destroy the information in this column?** Shuffle the column, score
the model again, and record the increase in error. Do it on data the model has not seen, and
do it many times, because the shuffle is random.

It is short enough to write out, which is worth doing once.

```{r}
#| label: permutation
baseline_rmse <- rmse_vec(test_set$abundance, predict(forest, test_set)$.pred)

permutation_importance <- function(model, data, outcome, repeats = 50) {
  baseline <- rmse_vec(data[[outcome]], predict(model, data)$.pred)
  map_dfr(setdiff(names(data), outcome), \(variable) {
    increases <- map_dbl(seq_len(repeats), \(i) {
      shuffled <- data
      shuffled[[variable]] <- sample(shuffled[[variable]])
      rmse_vec(data[[outcome]], predict(model, shuffled)$.pred) - baseline
    })
    tibble(variable = variable, increase = mean(increases),
           se = sd(increases) / sqrt(repeats))
  })
}

set.seed(3)
importance <- permutation_importance(forest, test_set, "abundance")

importance |>
  arrange(desc(increase)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 4)))
```

Note what changed. Substrate is now a single number rather than three dummies, because we
permuted the original column and let the recipe re-encode it. Splitting a categorical
variable's importance across its levels is a second, entirely avoidable way to make a real
effect look unimportant, and permuting before the recipe rather than after fixes it.

## Drawing the line

The three noise columns give us the scale the table was missing.

```{r}
#| label: fig-importance
#| fig-cap: "Permutation importance on 360 held-out stations, fifty shuffles each, with standard errors. The shaded band spans the three pure-noise columns: anything inside it is indistinguishable from a variable that cannot matter."
#| fig-alt: "A horizontal dot-and-error-bar plot of variables ordered by importance. Temperature is far out on its own at 0.185. Latitude, longitude, substrate and depth follow between 0.039 and 0.072, all clearly to the right of a grey shaded band. The band itself runs from about minus 0.015 to 0.029. Inside or touching it, in descending order, sit salinity, chlorophyll, survey year and season, together with the three noise columns which are drawn in a different colour."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5
noise_band <- importance |> filter(str_starts(variable, "noise_"))

importance |>
  mutate(kind = if_else(str_starts(variable, "noise_"), "pure noise", "measured"),
         variable = fct_reorder(variable, increase)) |>
  ggplot(aes(increase, variable, colour = kind)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = min(noise_band$increase), xmax = max(noise_band$increase),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#9aa5ad", alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#c9d1d7", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = increase - 2 * se, xmax = increase + 2 * se),
                 height = 0, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  labs(x = "increase in test RMSE when shuffled", y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

Five variables sit clearly outside the noise band: temperature, latitude, longitude,
substrate and depth. Four do not: salinity, chlorophyll, `survey_year` and season. The
correct sentence about the second group is not "these do not matter" — it is **"this model's
predictions do not depend on them any more than on a column of random numbers"**.

That reading is right for salinity and `survey_year`, which genuinely have no effect. It is
wrong for chlorophyll, which has a real, positive, saturating effect that we put there
ourselves. And before explaining chlorophyll, there is a more urgent question: how much of
this table is a property of the data, and how much is a property of the split we happened to
draw?

## One split is not a result

Everything above came from one 50/50 split. Repeat the whole procedure on eight different
splits and count how often each variable clears the highest of the three noise columns.

```{r}
#| label: across-splits
importance_for_split <- function(split_seed) {
  set.seed(split_seed)
  split <- initial_split(modelling, prop = 0.5)
  set.seed(2)
  fitted <- workflow() |>
    add_recipe(recipe(abundance ~ ., data = training(split)) |>
                 step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())) |>
    add_model(rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
                set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |> set_mode("regression")) |>
    fit(training(split))

  set.seed(3)
  scored <- permutation_importance(fitted, testing(split), "abundance", repeats = 15)
  ceiling <- max(scored$increase[str_starts(scored$variable, "noise_")])
  scored |> mutate(split = split_seed, rank = rank(-increase), noise_ceiling = ceiling)
}

repeated <- map_dfr(101:108, importance_for_split)

repeated |>
  filter(!str_starts(variable, "noise_")) |>
  summarise(`best rank` = min(rank), `worst rank` = max(rank),
            `splits above the noise ceiling` = sum(increase > noise_ceiling),
            `median increase` = round(median(increase), 3),
            .by = variable) |>
  arrange(`best rank`)
```

Chlorophyll comes first in one split and **eleventh in another**. Depth ranges from fifth to
twelfth. Season, longitude and latitude all move by five or six places. A variable-importance
figure built on a single split — which is what almost every one of them is — is reporting a
number with that much play in it and no indication of the fact.

One thing in the table is completely stable, and it is the thing that matters most:
**salinity and `survey_year` clear the noise ceiling in zero splits out of eight.** They are
the only two variables that never do, and they are exactly the two with no effect in the
generator. Every variable with a real effect clears it at least four times.

So the reliable output of this procedure is not a ranking. It is a **count**: how often does
this variable beat a column of random numbers? That is the number to put in a paper.

## Why chlorophyll is the unstable one

Chlorophyll in this simulation is generated from depth and season:
`exp(0.3 - 0.010 * depth + season_effect + noise)`. So almost everything chlorophyll knows
about abundance, depth and season also know. When we shuffle chlorophyll, the forest can
route the same information through the columns that are still intact — and whether it does
depends on which splits the trees happened to make on this particular training half.

Permutation importance measures **how much this model needs a column**, given the others. It
does not measure how much the variable matters in nature. With correlated predictors those
are different quantities, and the gap between them is not a defect of the method — it is the
question the method actually asks. Redundant variables sit near the boundary, which is
precisely why they are the ones whose rank swings.

Three practical consequences:

- A low importance means *redundant or unused*, never *unimportant*. Two columns carrying
  the same information will each score near zero, and which of them scores lower is
  arbitrary.
- A high importance means the model leans on that column. It says nothing about direction,
  shape, or causation — [the next page](partial-effects.qmd) is about recovering those.
- Importances are not comparable across models. Fit a linear model to the same data and the
  ranking changes, because a different model needs different columns.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The same thing from a maintained package
`vip::vi()` is the usual one-liner, but `vip` was archived from CRAN in 2026 and is no
longer maintained. `DALEX` with `DALEXtra`'s tidymodels adapter does model-agnostic
permutation importance and is actively developed.

```{r}
#| label: dalex
explainer <- explain_tidymodels(forest, data = select(test_set, -abundance),
                                y = test_set$abundance, verbose = FALSE)

set.seed(3)
parts <- model_parts(explainer, loss_function = loss_root_mean_square,
                     B = 25, type = "difference")

as_tibble(parts) |>
  filter(!variable %in% c("_full_model_", "_baseline_")) |>
  summarise(increase = round(mean(dropout_loss), 4), .by = variable) |>
  arrange(desc(increase)) |>
  slice_head(n = 6)
```

The same five variables, in the same order, at the same magnitudes — with `noise_3` sixth
in both.
:::

## Where this breaks down

**Importance is computed on a dataset, so it inherits that dataset's sampling.** If your
survey never visited water below 5 °C, temperature's importance describes the range you
sampled. §6's [extrapolation](../06-assumptions-limitations/sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd)
warning applies unchanged.

**Longitude and latitude ranked second and third.** They are not ecological drivers; they
are stand-ins for a smooth spatial field that no measured covariate explains. A model that
leans on coordinates is telling you there is structure you have not measured — which is
useful, and is not the same as "location matters".

**Shuffling creates impossible rows.** Permuting depth independently of temperature produces
20 m stations at 4 °C, which do not exist on this shelf, and the model is scored on its
predictions there. Accumulated local effects, on the next page, avoid this; conditional
permutation schemes exist too and are more work.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points

- **Always include a null column.** Three `rnorm()` columns ranked sixth, seventh and eighth
  of sixteen on impurity importance — above a real categorical effect, on every split we
  tried.
- **Impurity importance is biased towards continuous and many-levelled predictors.** It is
  the default. Do not use it for ranking.
- **Permutation importance on held-out data** answers a well-posed question and comes with a
  standard error. Permute the original column, before the recipe, so categorical variables
  are not split across dummies.
- **A single split is not a result.** Across eight splits chlorophyll's rank ran from first
  to eleventh and depth's from fifth to twelfth. Report the **count of splits in which a
  variable beats the noise ceiling**: the two predictors with no effect scored zero out of
  eight, and every real effect scored at least four.
- Write "the model relies on X", never "X drives Y".
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Refit with a boosted tree instead of a forest and recompute the permutation importance.
   Which variables change rank, and does the noise band move?
2. Drop `depth_m` from the recipe entirely and refit. Does chlorophyll's permutation
   importance rise, and by how much?
